New electric bikes

The future of cycling

Is an electric bike right for me?

If you’re looking for a quick, environmentally-friendly and economical way of getting from A-to-B, an electric bike could be a great option.

Electric bikes are pedal-powered like a conventional bicycle but assisted by an electric motor and rechargeable battery that help out at speeds of up to 15.5mph. This is often faster than the average person would cycle, especially in hilly terrain, so an e-bike could help you reach your destination a lot quicker than a traditional pedal bicycle.

There are lots of different types of electric bikes, including electric hybrid bikes, electric folding bikes, electric mountain bikes and e-cargo bikes. The different categories suit a wide range of activities from commuting to hardcore mountain biking.

Charging an electric bike at home and on the go

Electric bikes use regular three-pin plugs, compatible with domestic wall sockets. This means you won’t have to install charging points as you can charge an electric bike battery at home, or on the go.

Lots of electric bikes also come with removable batteries, which can offer extra flexibility on where you can charge.

Learn more about charging

Are electric bikes legal in the UK?

Electric bikes are legal in the UK, as long as you are 14 or older and the electric bike meets Electrically Assisted Pedal Cycle (EAPC) requirements. It is vital you buy your electric bike and electric bike battery from a reputable seller who makes sure that the electric bike not only meets the Electrically Assisted Pedal Cycle (EAPC) requirements but also follows the Construction and Use regulations, complies with the European standard EN15194 and contains a CE mark.

You don’t need a licence to ride one and it doesn’t need to be registered, taxed or insured.

Your questions answered

  • Electric bikes work just like a push bike and move as you pedal. But, an electric bike takes less effort as it also uses an electric motor, which is activated by a sensor when you start pedalling. For this reason, electric bikes are also known as pedal assist bikes, Electrically-assisted pedal cycles (EAPCs), or 'Pedelecs' – short for pedal electric cycles. electric bikes run on a battery that you need to charge to keep the electric bike going.

  • There are all sorts of electric bikes, just as there are various types of push bikes to suit different needs and lifestyles. Some common types of electric bikes include road electric bikes which are typically fitted with drop handlebars and quick on paved roads, off-road electric bikes suited to bumpy tracks in the forests or hills; hybrid electric bikes that combine the functionality of a road electric bike and an off-road electric bike and may come with features like conventional flat handlebars, mudguards, racks and bike lights. Folding electric bikes are meanwhile perfect for commuters who need to take them on the train or store them under their desk at work.

  • The cost of an electric bike depends upon the type and the number of features it offers. It can cost you as little as £500 or, at the top end, well over £10,000. electric bikes aimed at serious enthusiasts tend to be more expensive, with fancy frame materials like titanium or carbon fibre, hydraulic brakes, electrically operated gears and, for mountain bike versions, sophisticated suspension systems.

  • In the UK, electric bikes are limited to 15.5mph with electrically-assisted pedalling. Beyond this limit, the electric motor switches off and the electric bike operates as a regular push bike. So, you can ride an electric bike above 15.5mph, but only as fast as your legs can carry you!

  • You can charge your electric bike battery in three simple steps. First, make sure it's switched off. Then, connect the electric bike charger to a power socket and the battery pack. Finally, switch the power on to start charging the electric bike battery. Some electric bikes let you keep the battery pack attached to the bike and charge it from there, while others offer the option to remove it and charge separately from the bike. Most electric bikes have a light or charge status indicator on them to indicate when the battery is running low. 

  • The UK has its own laws on what can be classed as an electric bike and who can ride it. All road-legal electric bikes in the UK have pedals, and an electric motor of 250 Watts or less and can only go up to 15.5mph (25km/h). To ride an electric bike in the UK, you need to be at least 14 years old.

  • No, you don't need to tax or insure an electric bike to ride it in the UK. 

  • Electric bikes are legal in the UK if you are 14 or older and the electric bike meets Electrically Assisted Pedal Cycle (EAPC) requirements. It is vital you buy your electric bike and electric bike battery from a reputable seller who makes sure that the electric bike not only meets the Electrically Assisted Pedal Cycle (EAPC) requirements but also fulfils Construction and Use regulations and complies with European standard EN15194. It is reasonable to ask for evidence from the person or company you buy an electric bike from.
